blocks.x: Many renovation services in Winnipeg are honest and professional. But scams and bad operators exist, from fly-by-night crews to criminals who impersonate a real contractor and redirect your payments. Contractor payment fraud is a real risk. In one 2024 case, the Canadian Anti-Fraud Centre helped freeze a $615,820 transfer after a spear-phishing attack on a Canadian business.
Fake emails and invoices can look convincing. Here are eight red flags to watch for, and how to protect your project and your money.
1. A big cash deposit before any work
A reasonable deposit to order materials is normal. A large upfront payment in cash, especially before a contract is signed, is not. Tie payments to completed stages of work.
2. No written contract
If the scope, price, schedule and payment terms aren't in writing, you have little to enforce. A professional provider of renovation services will always put it on paper.
3. "We don't need a permit"
Some cosmetic work needs no permit, so [check what your project needs](/blog/winnipeg-renovation-permits). Where one is required, skipping it saves the contractor time, not you.

If undeclared work is found, the City may issue notices or orders, and fines or penalties may apply. Unpermitted work can also get in the way of a sale or lease, and leave you responsible for fixing it later.
4. No WCB clearance or insurance

For businesses, WCB Manitoba warns of a direct cost: hiring a contractor who isn't in good standing might leave them liable for its assessment costs. Its warning doesn't mention homeowners, who can ask WCB about their own situation.

WCB's public Clearance Request System lets anyone print [a clearance letter](/blog/how-to-check-a-contractors-wcb-clearance-manitoba), so do that before work starts and before each payment. Ask for a certificate of liability insurance as well.
5. Door-to-door or high-pressure offers
"We're working in the area and have leftover materials" or "this price is only good today" are classic pressure tactics. Legitimate contractors give you time to compare quotes.
6. Payment details that change by email

Payment redirection is a real risk. The Canadian Anti-Fraud Centre says Canadian businesses reported losing more than $58 million to spear phishing in 2023. An attack might look like a supplier or contractor emailing to request urgent payment to an alternate bank account.

Criminals hack or imitate a contractor's email, sometimes from a look-alike domain, and send "updated" banking instructions. Before you pay any new account, **call the contractor at a phone number you already have**, not one in the email.
7. Pressure to pay outside normal channels
Requests for e-transfers to a personal name, gift cards or cryptocurrency, or payments to an account in a different name than the company, should stop you cold.
8. No public record or references
Most businesses show up in public records. Search the name on the contract in the [Manitoba Companies Office](https://companiesoffice.gov.mb.ca/) registry, and ask for references you can call.

A sole owner trading under their own name doesn't have to register a business name, so a missing name is a reason to ask, not proof of fraud. If the name doesn't match or no one can vouch for the work, keep looking.
How to protect every contractor payment
Agree on a payment schedule in the contract, tied to milestones.

Hold back 7.5% of each payment and keep it for at least 60 days after substantial performance is certified or the work is completed or abandoned, whichever comes first, as The Builders' Liens Act requires. It's paid later, not a discount. Deal with deficiencies separately in your contract.
Verify any change in payment details by phone using a known number.
Pay by traceable methods and keep receipts.
Use multi-factor authentication on your own email accounts.
If something goes wrong
If you think you've been targeted, contact your bank immediately, then report it to the Canadian Anti-Fraud Centre and your local police. Speed matters for recovering funds.
The bottom line
Good renovation services are transparent: written contracts, permits where they're required and clear payment terms. Anything less is a warning sign.
